native_result.query: What is the average length of original papers in Experimental Economics and that in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB:
RESULT — Average length of original papers: Experimental Economics vs Psychology

FINAL ANSWER (natural-language, grounded in the data):
Original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology. In the dataset, the 18 Experimental Economics originals (project 'ee') average 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.4, range 16–45), whereas the 97 Psychology originals (project 'rpp') average only 11.2 pages (median 9, SD 6.3, range 1–31) — a gap of roughly 16.8 pages, i.e., economics originals are about 2.5× longer on average. The rpp mean is inflated relative to its median because of short-format articles: 42.3% of rpp papers are ≤7 pages and 55.7% are ≤10 pages (several are just 1–3 pages, reflecting short-report journal formats), which drags the mean down toward the short end while the median (9 pages) better represents the typical paper. Even so, the contrast is robust: by any measure (mean or median), Experimental Economics originals are far longer than Psychology originals in these replication projects.

SUPPORTING TABLE (unique-original level, one value per 'id'):

| Project                        | n (unique originals) | mean  | median | sd   | min | max |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|-------|--------|------|-----|-----|
| Experimental Economics (ee)    | 18                   | 28.00 | 27.5   | 7.37 | 16  | 45  |
| Psychology (rpp)               | 97                   | 11.22 | 9.0    | 6.30 | 1   | 31  |

Headline difference: 28.00 − 11.22 = 16.78 pages.

SENSITIVITY (U1) — Psychology bucket including Many Labs originals (ml1+ml3+rpp, 123 unique ids; 117 after title-dedup):
- Psychology incl. Many Labs: mean 11.07, median 9, SD 6.45, range 1–31 (title-dedup mean 11.16). Conclusion unchanged: ee ≈ 28 pages vs Psychology ≈ 11 pages regardless of whether Many Labs is included.

EXECUTION-VERIFIED CHECKS:
- A4 (drop flag): 7 rpp ids ARE flagged drop=True (rpp.154, rpp.46, rpp.59, rpp.69, rpp.73, rpp.77, rpp.82); 0 ee rows are dropped. Applying the flag would shrink the rpp sample from 97 to 90 originals and shift the rpp mean from 11.22 to 11.00 pages (median unchanged at 9). I retained all 97 in the primary result because 'drop' flags meta-analysis exclusions of O/R pairs (e.g., effect-estimation issues), not problems with the original papers themselves; the conclusion is insensitive either way.
- Duplicate handling: 'length' is constant within every 'id' (verified: 0 ids with >1 distinct length), and ee/rpp have exactly 1 row per id, so unique-original averaging equals all-rows averaging for the headline. For ml1/ml3 in the sensitivity bucket, I used the unique-id level (equivalently the aggregated=True rows).
- Data quality: length has no missing, zero, negative, or non-numeric values in ee or rpp; 1–3-page values (e.g., rpp.53 = 1, ml1.10 = 1) are genuine short-format articles and were retained.

WORKFLOW: pandas script analysis/average_paper_length.py — loads the study CSV (927 rows × 57 cols, 141 unique ids), verifies within-id constancy of length and the drop-flag status for rpp/ee, filters project ∈ {ee, rpp}, dedupes by 'id', computes mean/median/SD/min/max/n per project, and re-computes the Psychology bucket including ml1/ml3 (plus a title-dedup check) as the U1 sensitivity.

ASSUMPTIONS APPLIED: "Psychology" = project 'rpp' (with ml1/ml3 shown separately as sensitivity); average = arithmetic mean over unique originals; no outlier trimming; 'drop' flag not applied in the primary estimate (impact quantified: rpp mean 11.22 → 11.00 if applied).

LIMITATIONS: page counts are as recorded in the curated dataset and not externally validated; the rpp sample is dominated by 2008 short-format psychology articles, so the mean–median gap (11.2 vs 9) reflects journal format as much as discipline norms; the ee sample is small (n=18), so its mean carries more sampling uncertainty.

FINAL ANSWER (natural-language, grounded in the data):
Original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology. In the dataset, the 18 Experimental Economics originals (project 'ee') average 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.4, range 16–45), whereas the 97 Psychology originals (project 'rpp') average only 11.2 pages (median 9, SD 6.3, range 1–31) — a gap of roughly 16.8 pages, i.e., economics originals are about 2.5× longer on average. The rpp mean is inflated relative to its median because of short-format articles: 42.3% of rpp papers are ≤7 pages and 55.7% are ≤10 pages (several are just 1–3 pages, reflecting short-report journal formats), which drags the mean down toward the short end while the median (9 pages) better represents the typical paper. Even so, the contrast is robust: by any measure (mean or median), Experimental Economics originals are far longer than Psychology originals in these replication projects.
